children: Democratic lawmakers preparing to take control of Congress in January said Sunday they would investigate Elon Musk, scrutinize corporate conduct and examine decisions by senior Trump administration officials.

For investors, the planned inquiries could bring legal expenses, disclosure demands and reputational risks for companies drawn into congressional investigations. Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s (D-Mass.) expected leadership of the Senate Banking Committee puts financial services oversight in focus, although she identified no corporate targets.
"If you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you'd better get ready for some investigations, serious ones," Warren told CBS’s “Face the Nation.”

Rep. Robert Garcia, expected to chair the House Oversight Committee, said lawmakers would examine Musk’s involvement in federal workforce cuts through the Department of Government Efficiency. He also plans to investigate newly appointed White House chief of staff Stephen Miller’s role in immigration enforcement.
"I think there's a lot of interest, not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress to speak to Mr. Musk," Garcia told CNN’s “State of the Union.”

The comments didn't establish whether any Musk-led companies would face investigations. They nevertheless suggest his government activities will receive greater scrutiny following Democrats’ midterm victories.

Incoming House speaker Hakeem Jeffries also backed an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, citing his management of the Iran war. The conflict has driven gasoline prices higher, adding an economic dimension to the political confrontation.
"Pete Hegseth has got to go," Jeffries told ABC’s “This Week.” House impeachment would not itself remove Hegseth; removal would require conviction in the Senate.
Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated the administration would resist the planned investigations.
"If that's what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready," he said.

title: Democrats signal Musk, corporate probes as investors face new oversight risks
